Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Omar, a 38-year-old single man with a warm smile and skilled hands, used to take immense pride in his work as a hairdresser. His salon, bustling with clients and lively chatter, was his sanctuary. But a year and a half ago, his world irrevocably shifted. It began with a sudden, excruciating pain in his abdomen while he was styling a client’s hair. One moment, he was discussing highlights, the next, he was collapsing, his vision blurring as waves of nausea and agony consumed him. He was rushed to the emergency room, where doctors discovered a severe, rapidly progressing internal infection that required immediate, life-saving surgery. The days that followed were a blur of antiseptic smells, beeping machines, and a constant, searing pain that seemed to consume his entire being. He remembered the metallic tang of hospital air, the sterile scent clinging to everything, and the sharp, burning sensation of the incision site.

Even now, long after his physical recovery, the memory of that time still manifests in vivid, unsettling ways. Sometimes, without warning, the faint, acrid smell of hospital disinfectant will suddenly flood his senses, even when he’s simply walking down a street or preparing coffee in his kitchen. More disturbingly, when he thinks about the terrifying event, a phantom pain will erupt in his lower abdomen, mimicking the precise, agonizing ache he felt immediately after surgery. These sensations often bring with them a rush of intense emotion; sometimes, he'll be overwhelmed by a profound sense of horror and helplessness, a feeling so potent it takes his breath away, yet without any accompanying image or clear memory of the operating room itself. He just *feels* it, intensely.

Omar’s body, once a reliable tool for his craft, now feels like a stranger, an adversary. He has come to believe that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger, even when he is safe. This conviction is reinforced by a constant, underlying tension in his muscles, a persistent feeling that his body is on alert, ready to react to danger at any moment. This vigilance makes him jumpy. Just last week, a client showing him vacation photos on her phone scrolled past an image of a hospital corridor where her friend worked. The sterile white walls and fluorescent lighting, even in a small picture, sent a jolt through Omar. His heart pounded, his palms grew sweaty, and he had to excuse himself for a moment, the strong physical reaction leaving him shaken. He worries constantly that his reactions since the event mean that he is going crazy, that he is losing his grip on reality.

His nights offer little respite. Waking up from a nightmare, often one he can’t quite recall but leaves a palpable residue of terror, is a regular occurrence. The lingering fear and exhaustion make it hard to start his day, adding to his already heightened state of alert. He finds himself actively avoiding anything that might trigger these reactions. He’s stopped looking at news articles about health crises, has muted keywords on social media, and has even started to avoid going for his routine follow-up check-ups, dreading the thought of undergoing another medical examination or procedure. He feels a deep fear of the vulnerability that comes with being examined, a fear that his body will betray him again.

This pervasive fear and constant state of readiness have taken a toll on Omar’s life, particularly his work. His usual easygoing demeanor has been replaced by a subtle irritability, and his clients, though loyal, have noticed his occasional distractedness. He finds it harder to focus, his mind often drifting to monitoring his own internal sensations, trying to discern if the slightest ache or twinge is a sign of another impending catastrophe. He has come to believe he can no longer trust his own body, which now feels like an unpredictable enemy. The joy he once derived from his craft is often overshadowed by this internal struggle. He finally sought help, exhausted by the relentless cycle of fear, physical reactivity, and the profound sense that his own body has turned against him, desperate to find a way to reclaim himself and his life from the shadow of that terrifying event.
